passage: Maria, you're a tired mother, I can see it. Little Zaid is talking like a baby again since his sister came? Listen to your old Nani Dilnaz. I was twenty-four when Samira was born, and your uncle Farhad, who was three and a half, suddenly wanted his bottle back and started saying "me tiny". My mother-in-law said, "Laugh at him, he'll stop." I didn't. I gave him extra cuddles and even let him have milk in the bottle at bedtime. But I kept everything else the same: breakfast at seven, the park at five, bath, story, bed. He needed to know two things, that he was still loved and that his world hadn't fallen apart. In about a month he told me, "I'm the big brother now," and gave the bottle to the baby. So cuddle Zaid. Keep the routine. He'll find his way back.

qa.q: What did Farhad start saying when Samira was born?
qa.a: "Me tiny."

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz refuse to laugh at Farhad, as her mother-in-law suggested?
qa.a: She believed he needed to feel loved and safe, and mocking would have told him the opposite.

qa.q: Which choices helped Farhad move forward, and why?
qa.a: Extra cuddles and the bedtime bottle met his need to be babied, while the steady routine showed his world was still in place, so he could step into being the big brother.

qa.q: How might Maria feel after hearing this story?
qa.a: Probably reassured and less worried about Zaid, with a clear plan: cuddle him, keep the routine and give it time. 🤍

grounding: A grandmother recalls meeting her young son's baby-like behaviour after a sibling's birth with cuddles and steady routines, and passes this on to her granddaughter.

Since Lakshmi started night shifts at the hospital laundry, she had forty minutes between getting home and dropping Sangeeta at the anganwadi. And for a week now, Sangeeta, four, who had been dressing herself since summer, lay on the floor every morning saying, "Baby can't do buttons," in a tiny voice.
Lakshmi's back ached, and the bus was at 8:10. She knelt anyway. "Baby can't do buttons? Then Amma will help this once." She did two buttons, cuddled her, and let Sangeeta do the last one. "Clever baby."
Breakfast was the same idli on the same steel plate, and the same song on the way to the bus stop. She didn't laugh, and she didn't skip the routine. By Friday, Sangeeta announced, "I'm big today," and buttoned everything herself, crookedly.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta say in a tiny voice every morning?
qa.a: "Baby can't do buttons."

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta be acting like a baby since Lakshmi started night shifts?
qa.a: She may be missing her mother and want to feel looked after, so being small is her way of asking for closeness.

qa.q: What choice did Lakshmi make despite the 8:10 bus, and why did it work?
qa.a: She knelt, helped with two buttons, cuddled her and kept breakfast and the song the same, so Sangeeta felt both cared for and safe, and was 'big' again by Friday.

qa.q: What would change if Lakshmi had said, 'Stop acting like a baby, we're late'?
qa.a: Sangeeta would probably feel more anxious and cling harder, and the baby behaviour might last longer.

grounding: A mother short on time after night shifts meets her four-year-old's baby-like behaviour with a cuddle and patience while keeping the morning routine steady.

In their flat in Andheri, six-year-old Tejas had started wetting the bed again, three weeks after joining Class 1 at a new school. He wanted Vinita to feed him with her hand at dinner, and he crawled into her lap during homework.
Their neighbour, dropping off a tiffin, joked, "Such a big boy wanting to be fed!" Tejas's face crumpled.

A fortnight later, Tejas pushed her hand away at dinner. "I'll eat by myself, Mumma. You watch."

qa.a: He felt ashamed and exposed, since his need for babying was being laughed at while he was already stressed by the new school.

qa.q: Which of Vinita's choices helped Tejas move forward, and why?
qa.a: Protecting him from the joke, changing the sheets without blame and keeping the evening routine steady, so he felt safe enough to eat by himself a fortnight later.

qa.q: How might the neighbour have felt when Vinita said, 'We're having cuddly weeks'?
qa.a: The neighbour may have realised the joke landed badly and understood that Tejas needed kindness, not teasing.

grounding: A mother answers her six-year-old's return to bed-wetting and wanting to be fed with patience and cuddles, without mocking, while keeping routines steady.

passage:
Looking back at last spring, I'm glad I trusted my instinct. After Thatha died, Keerthana, six, went backwards overnight. She sucked her thumb again, asked me to feed her rice with my hand, and climbed into my bed every night at two.
My mother-in-law said, "Ayesha, you're spoiling her. At six?" A neighbour laughed and called her "baby Keerthu". I asked them, gently, not to tease her.
I fed her when she asked. I let her into my bed. I cuddled her more than ever. But I kept everything else the same: school bus at seven-forty, bath before dinner, one story, lights out. She needed something to stay put while so much had changed.
About five weeks in, she pushed my hand away at dinner. "I can do it, Amma." I pretended to be busy so she wouldn't see me tear up.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do every night at two?
qa.a: She climbed into her Amma's bed every night at two.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana have wanted to be fed by hand after Thatha died?
qa.a: The loss shook her sense of safety, and being cared for like a little one again reassured her that Amma was still there to look after her.

qa.q: Which of Ayesha's choices helped Keerthana move forward sooner?
qa.a: Pairing extra cuddles and feeding with an unchanged routine, the same bus, bath, one story and lights out, so comfort and steadiness came together.

qa.q: What would change for Keerthana if the teasing about "baby Keerthu" had gone on?
qa.a: Keerthana might have felt ashamed of needing comfort and hidden her fear, which could have made the clinging last longer.

grounding: Illustrates a parent who answers her grieving child's baby-like behaviour with warmth and no mockery while keeping daily routines steady, and sees the child move forward.

passage:
Diary, Wednesday. Leela.

Elizabeth, my five-year-old, has been wetting the bed again since her baby brother arrived. And speaking like a baby, "Lizzie want Mummy do it," for everything, even shoes.

My mother-in-law said I should tell her to stop behaving like a baby. I didn't. I remember being the older child myself.

So I did two things. Extra cuddles, especially at bedtime. I sat on her bed longer than usual and told her how much I love our time together. And I kept everything else the same: school at eight, the same lunchbox, the same bedtime song. When she wet the bed, I changed the sheets without a word.

Today she put on her own shoes and said, "I'm big again, Mummy." I nearly cried.

Warmth plus the same old routines. It's working.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth put on by herself today?
qa.a: Her own shoes.

qa.q: Why did Leela ignore the advice to tell Elizabeth to stop?
qa.a: Leela felt protective and understanding, remembering being the older child, and believed mocking would only make Elizabeth more anxious.

qa.q: Why is changing the sheets without a word a wise choice?
qa.a: It avoids shame and keeps things calm, so Elizabeth doesn't feel in trouble for something she can't help right now.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel saying "I'm big again"?
qa.a: Elizabeth likely feels proud and secure, reassured that she's still loved even with the new baby.

grounding: Shows a parent meeting a child's regression with extra cuddles and patience while keeping routines steady, and the child moving forward.

In the Gothenburg winter dark, Jin had started wetting the bed again and talking in a squeaky baby voice at dinner. It began the week he moved up to the big-kids group at preschool.

His grandmother suggested a sticker chart and "no more baby nonsense." Ulla thought about it and chose differently. When Jin said, "Jin want uppy," she picked him up without comment. She changed the sheets calmly at night, no sighing, and let him sleep with the old giraffe.

But dinner stayed at six, bath at seven, two books, lights out. And every morning she walked him to the big-kids room and said, "I'll be back after snack time. You can tell me one thing you did."

By the end of January the squeaky voice had faded, and Jin was telling her three things, not one.

qa.a: It began the week he moved up to the big-kids group at preschool.

qa.q: Why did Ulla decide against the sticker chart and "no more baby nonsense"?
qa.a: Ulla felt tender and patient, sensing Jin was anxious about the big-kids group and needed comfort rather than pressure.

qa.q: What did Ulla combine that helped Jin move forward?
qa.a: Ulla combined warm pick-ups and calm night-time care with steady routines: dinner at six, bath at seven, two books and the morning walk.

qa.q: How might Jin feel when Ulla picks him up without comment?
qa.a: Jin probably feels safe and accepted, which helps him face the new group and slowly drop the baby voice.

I cried in the car, the happy kind.
